---
name: interface-density-preference
description: "The user prefers compact, consolidated interfaces and expects every panel or control to justify its space."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  pinned: false
  originSessionId: 015dae9d-ee04-45fa-86ea-f0362570ddee
  modified: 2026-09-21T23:40:24.756Z
---

When reviewing interfaces built for them, the user consistently pushes toward
density and consolidation. Across a single session they asked to merge separate
slider controls into the chart axes those sliders drove, to show two related
values in one section rather than behind a toggle button, and then to delete a
second large visualization on the grounds that it might not be worth its space.

The underlying preference is that each panel, control, and visualization must
earn its area. Two controls that set the same value are redundant; a toggle that
hides half the data is worse than showing both; and a large view whose main
result is negative ("nothing is wrong here") should be replaced by something
smaller that carries the same contrast.

Consequences for building interfaces for this user: default to fewer, denser
views rather than more panels. Prefer making an existing element interactive
over adding a separate control beside it. Before adding a second instance of any
visualization, ask what it shows that the first does not, and if the answer is
only a contrast, look for a compact readout that carries the same contrast
instead. Expect to be asked to remove things, so propose the smaller version
first.

input.prompt:
Work in ~/workspace/chronoscope (React + TypeScript + Vite, Vitest). This is Chronoscope, a tool comparing bitemporal storage representations.

READ FIRST, to absorb conventions:
- src/core/types.ts, src/core/log.ts, src/core/reference.ts
- src/core/strategies/index.ts (Strategy interface, OpCounts, Config, materialize)
- src/core/strategies/registry.ts (STRATEGIES, AnyStrategy)
- src/core/strategies/deltas.ts, intervals.ts, snapshots.ts, hybrid.ts, snapshotStale.ts (the five state shapes you must render)
- src/ui/TwinTimelines.tsx and src/ui/Readout.tsx (component style)
- src/ui/scale.ts, src/ui/palette.ts (use seriesColour for per-strategy colour)
- src/ui/render.test.tsx (the static-render test pattern — follow it)
- src/styles.css (use existing classes: .panel, .num, .tag, table styles)

YOUR TASK: the strategy comparison band — one row per strategy, all five reacting to the same facts.

FILES YOU OWN (create only these; edit no other file):
- src/ui/StrategyRow.tsx
- src/ui/internals/EventList.tsx
- src/ui/internals/IntervalRows.tsx
- src/ui/internals/SnapshotStack.tsx
- src/ui/internals/index.tsx
- src/ui/StrategyRow.test.tsx

=== StrategyRow ===
Props:
  { strategy: AnyStrategy, log: readonly Fact[], config: Config,
    validCursor: Day, systemCursor: Day, horizon: {start,end} }

It must compute, internally:
- the materialised state: materialize(strategy, log, config)
- the value this strategy returns for EACH attribute in ATTRS at (validCursor, systemCursor)
- the oracle's answer via referenceQuery, and whether they agree
- the ops the LAST fact in the log cost: materialize over log.slice(0,-1), then
  strategy.apply(thatState, lastFact, config) and read .ops. Guard the empty log.
- strategy.size(state) — records stored

Render compactly, one row:
- a 3px colour bar or dot in seriesColour(strategy.key), plus name and blurb
- the value per attribute, and an agreement marker. When it disagrees with the
  oracle, show what the oracle said too, using the .tag.wrong class. Getting this
  wrong is the whole point of the tool, so make disagreement unmissable but not
  garish.
- last-fact ops as three small numbers with labels: written / rewritten / invalidated
- records stored
- the internal state, rendered natively (below)

The user of this project strongly prefers dense, compact interfaces — every
element must earn its space. No decorative chrome, no duplicated controls, no
large empty panels.

=== Internal state renderers ===
internals/index.tsx exports a single function that picks the right renderer for a
strategy key and returns null for an unknown one:
  renderInternals(key: string, state: unknown, props: {horizon, validCursor, systemCursor}): ReactNode

- EventList: for 'deltas'. A compact table of facts — attr, value, valid, system.
  Dim facts whose systemTime is after systemCursor (not yet recorded).
- IntervalRows: for 'intervals'. Each row of IntervalState drawn as a horizontal
  bar positioned by validFrom/validTo on a shared x scale over the horizon (use
  linear() from ../scale), labelled with its value. Rows still open in system
  time (systemTo === INF) render solid; rows closed in system time render faded
  — that is the audit trail, and seeing closed rows accumulate under a
  retroactive write is the point of this renderer.
- SnapshotStack: for 'snapshots', 'hybrid' and 'snapshotStale'. A compact list of
  snapshots: validAt, the attribute values it holds, and its system range. Faded
  when closed. For snapshotStale, a stale snapshot is one still open whose stored
  values disagree with referenceQuery at (its validAt, systemCursor) — mark those
  with the .tag.wrong class. That marking is what makes the bug visible in the
  storage itself rather than only in the answer.

Keep each renderer scrollable with max-height rather than letting a long history
blow out the layout — arbitrary facts can be injected at runtime.

Note INF is exported from src/core/types.ts. Values are number | string; format
numbers with toLocaleString('en-GB').

=== TESTING (StrategyRow.test.tsx) ===
Use renderToStaticMarkup exactly as src/ui/render.test.tsx does (the file is
.tsx, vitest is configured for it). Required:
- every strategy in STRATEGIES renders without throwing, on SCENARIO, and the
  markup contains no 'NaN' and no 'Infinity'
- each renders on an EMPTY log without throwing
- the four correct strategies show no disagreement marker on SCENARIO at
  (1 May 2026, 10 June 2026) — use day() from core/dates
- snapshotStale DOES show a disagreement at that coordinate, and the markup
  contains both its wrong answer (60,000) and the oracle's (72,000)
- the intervals renderer shows more rows after the backdated fact than before it
  (closed rows accumulate rather than being mutated away)
- ops for the last fact are rendered, and for SCENARIO the last fact is the
  backdated raise, so snapshots must show a non-zero invalidated count while
  deltas shows zero

Verify before finishing:
  npx vitest run src/ui/StrategyRow.test.tsx
  npx tsc --noEmit
Both clean. Iterate until they pass. Do NOT git commit. Do NOT edit App.tsx —
I wire it up.

Report back: your exact prop signatures, the renderInternals signature, and
anything you had to decide that the brief left open.

  its own beyond uncommitted form fields.

rather than the boundary.

- src/ui/Sandbox.tsx
- src/ui/Sandbox.test.tsx

=== Props ===
  { state: AppState, dispatch: (a: Action) => void }
Import both types from '../state'. Add nothing to the reducer — every action you
need already exists: addFact, advanceClock, setSnapshotInterval, undo, reset.

=== What it must offer ===
1. Add a fact: attribute (a select over ATTRS), value, and valid time. Valid time
   is freely chosen anywhere in HORIZON, past or future — that is the whole
   point. Use a date-ish control; a range slider over HORIZON with the formatted
   date shown beside it is fine and matches the rest of the interface.
   Salary takes a number, manager takes text. Switch the input by attribute.

   fixed steps (e.g. +1 day, +1 week, +1 month) is plenty.
   CRITICAL, and the thing to get right: a fact is always recorded AT the clock,
   never before it. The form must make an illegal system time unexpressible
   rather than validating it after the fact. Show the user, in plain words, that
   the fact they are about to add will be recorded at the clock's current date.
   Explain in one short line why system time cannot be chosen freely: it is the
   record of what we did, and a store that lets you write into its own past has
   stopped being an audit log.
3. Snapshot interval slider — every snapshot and hybrid cost depends on it.
4. Undo the last fact, and reset to the scenario. Disable undo on an empty log.

element must earn its space. One tight panel, controls on as few rows as
possible. No decorative chrome, no duplicated controls, no large empty areas.

component is a pure function of props plus local form state, test the LOGIC by

  a fact added after advancing the clock carries the clock's systemTime; adding
  a fact never produces a systemTime earlier than the log's latest; undo then
  add still yields a legal log (append does not throw MonotonicSystemTimeError)
- adding a fact with a valid time in the future and one in the past both succeed
- a property-ish loop: apply 50 pseudo-random legal action sequences (mix of
  addFact, advanceClock, undo) to the reducer starting from initialState() and
  assert after each step that the log's systemTimes are non-decreasing and that
  clock >= latestSystemTime(log). Seed it so failures reproduce.

Verify before finishing:
  npx vitest run src/ui/Sandbox.test.tsx
  npx tsc --noEmit
Both clean. Iterate until they pass. Do NOT git commit. Do NOT edit App.tsx or
src/state.ts — I wire it up.

Report back: your prop signature, how you made an illegal system time
unexpressible in the form, and anything the brief left open that you decided.

content.text:
The app is whole. 359 tests, pushed, deploy running — reload **http://localhost:5173/chronoscope/** to see it now, or the live URL in a minute.

**What's on the page:** logical history (both values, draggable axes), sandbox controls, five strategy rows, scale band.

Three things from this block worth your attention:

**The strategy rows show internal state natively**, which is where the argument actually lands. Intervals draws closed rows *fading rather than disappearing*, so you watch the audit trail accumulate under a retroactive write. The snapshot stack marks its own stale entries — so the bug is visible in the storage, not just in the wrong answer.

**I corrected hybrid's notation from `O(1)` to `O(1 + A/k)`.** It's flat in the number of facts, but the scheduled grid snapshot is A records amortised over a k-day cell. Labelling it `O(1)` would let someone skimming the table read it as equivalent to deltas' genuinely constant append — the one comparison in that row that can't be fudged. The panel now also states outright that its notation measures growth in N, with attributes and horizon held fixed, which was a real ambiguity.

**The sandbox has no system-time control at all** — not a disabled one, not a validated one. The `addFact` action has no `systemTime` field, so the reducer stamps the clock. The invariant is enforced by the type rather than by a check, which is a better answer than "we validate it" if you get asked.

Remaining from the plan: the guided narrative stepper, and a pass on whether the scale band earns its space now that you've seen it.

- src/ui/StrategyRow.tsx (the caller)
- src/core/strategies/intervals.ts (Interval shape), src/core/strategies/snapshots.ts (Snapshot shape)
- src/core/types.ts (INF), src/core/dates.ts (formatDay, formatDayLong)
- src/ui/StrategyRow.test.tsx (existing tests you must keep passing)
- src/styles.css

The user reviewed the running app and gave two specific corrections. Both are
about the storage views looking like *real storage* rather than like diagrams.

- src/ui/internals/IntervalRows.tsx
- src/ui/internals/SnapshotStack.tsx
- src/ui/internals/internals.test.tsx  (new)

=== CORRECTION 1: intervals must look like a bitemporal table ===
User's words: "interval storage representation with the rectangles looks good but
is not realistic, better to use [start,end) kind of format?"

Replace the bar/rectangle drawing with a real TABLE, the way a bitemporal table
actually reads. Columns: attribute, value, valid range, system range. Render
ranges in half-open interval notation, literally:
  [15 Jan, 1 Mar)     and for an open end:   [10 Jun, ∞)
Use INF from core/types to detect an open end. The half-open notation is not
decoration — it is why adjacent rows share a boundary without overlapping, and
it should be legible at a glance that one row's end is the next row's start.

Keep: rows closed in system time render faded (that is the audit trail), open
rows solid. Sort stably (attribute, then validFrom, then systemFrom). Keep the
max-height scroll so an injected history cannot blow out the layout.

Add a one-line caption explaining what a reader is looking at: that a
retroactive write does not mutate a row, it closes it in system time and opens
replacements, so the old belief stays queryable.

=== CORRECTION 2: the snapshot system column is confusing ===
User's words: "in the snapshot storage representation what is the meaning of
system column. I would expect only to have the time that has been registered in
the system, not with the `...` of `10 Jun–…`"

The range presentation is the problem. Change to:
- a "recorded" column showing ONLY systemFrom (the moment that snapshot was
  written) — that is what the reader expects and what the column name implies
- a separate, explicit status: snapshots still current show nothing extra;
  snapshots that have been superseded show "superseded <date>" using systemTo,
  and stay faded.
Do not silently drop systemTo — a superseded snapshot is still queryable at an
earlier system time, and that is the strategy's whole point. Just stop
presenting it as an open-ended range in a column headed "system".

Keep the existing stale marking for snapshotStale (checkStale), which uses
.tag.wrong — that is working and the user did not complain about it.

=== TESTING (internals.test.tsx) ===
Follow the static-render pattern in src/ui/render.test.tsx exactly
(renderToStaticMarkup). Build states via materialize() from
core/strategies/index over SCENARIO. Required:
- IntervalRows renders half-open notation: markup contains '[' and ')' around
  formatted dates, and contains '∞' for at least one open row
- adjacent rows for one attribute share a boundary: assert some row's validTo
  string appears as another row's validFrom
- IntervalRows shows more rows after SCENARIO's backdated fact than for a log
  without it (closed rows accumulate rather than being mutated away)
- SnapshotStack shows a recorded date per snapshot and NEVER renders an
  open-ended range dash for the system column
- SnapshotStack marks superseded snapshots with the word 'superseded'
- snapshotStale still marks stale snapshots with the wrong tag
- both render on an empty log without throwing; no 'NaN', no 'Infinity'

Verify before finishing:
  npx vitest run src/ui/internals.test.tsx src/ui/StrategyRow.test.tsx
  npx tsc --noEmit
Both clean, and StrategyRow.test.tsx must still pass unchanged. Iterate until
green. Do NOT git commit.

The user strongly prefers dense, compact interfaces — every element earns its
space. No decorative chrome.

Report back: what you changed in each file, and anything the brief left open
that you decided.

input.description: Event-based snapshot grid and cost ranges
input.prompt:
Work in ~/workspace/chronoscope (React + TypeScript + Vite, Vitest). Chronoscope compares bitemporal storage representations.

READ FIRST:
- src/core/strategies/hybrid.ts  (the strategy you are changing)
- src/core/strategies/index.ts   (Config, Strategy, materialize)
- src/core/strategies/snapshots.ts (Snapshot type, liveSnapshot helper it shares)
- src/core/log.ts, src/core/reference.ts, src/core/gen.ts
- src/core/registry.test.ts and src/core/snapshots.test.ts (the property sweeps that MUST stay green)
- src/core/cost.ts and src/core/cost.test.ts and src/core/costClaims.test.ts
- src/ui/CostPanel.tsx

The user reviewed the running app and said: "the snapshot interval and
retroactive depth need to swing with much bigger numbers (probably snapshot
interval needs to be renamed in number of events or something like this?)"

They are right, and the fix is semantic rather than cosmetic. A snapshot grid
measured in CALENDAR DAYS over a fixed horizon cannot scale with a history of
10,000 facts — the grid stops meaning anything. Real systems snapshot every k
EVENTS. Change the model to match.

FILES YOU OWN (edit only these):
- src/core/strategies/hybrid.ts
- src/core/cost.ts
- src/core/cost.test.ts
- src/core/costClaims.test.ts   (only if a claim's wording needs updating; keep its guarantees)
- src/ui/CostPanel.tsx
- src/core/hybrid.test.ts       (new, if you want extra coverage)
Do NOT edit: snapshots.ts, snapshotStale.ts, deltas.ts, intervals.ts, registry.ts,
index.ts, log.ts, reference.ts, state.ts, or any other UI file. Do NOT edit
registry.test.ts or snapshots.test.ts — they must pass UNCHANGED.

=== 1. hybrid.ts: grid by events, not by days ===
Config.snapshotInterval keeps its name but now means "one snapshot every k
distinct valid times", not "every k days". Update its doc comment in
strategies/index.ts... ACTUALLY no: you may not edit index.ts. Instead document
the new meaning thoroughly in hybrid.ts itself.

New grid: take the distinct validFrom values present in the log, sorted
ascending, and snapshot at every k-th of them. That grid grows with the history
instead of being pinned to a calendar, which is the whole point of the change.

Everything else about the strategy stays: snapshots are bitemporal (closed in
system time rather than mutated); a retroactive fact invalidates and rebuilds
grid snapshots at or after its valid time; a read takes the nearest live grid
snapshot at or before the query's valid time and replays the log forward from
there, bounded by the gap to the next grid point.

CRITICAL: hybrid must remain CORRECT. registry.test.ts and snapshots.test.ts
sweep it against the oracle at every critical point over the scenario and 30+
generated histories, for several snapshotInterval values. Those must stay green
without being touched. If a grid point set can be empty (k larger than the
number of distinct valid times), the read must still be correct — fall back to
replaying the log from the beginning.

=== 2. cost.ts: re-derive hybrid's formulas in N ===
With an event-based grid the horizon drops out of hybrid's model entirely:
- snapshot count is now N/k rather than H/k
- the replay window is ~k facts rather than (N/H)*k
Rewrite hybrid's storage / read / append / retro and their notation strings
accordingly, keeping the same commenting discipline the file already uses
(explain what each term counts and why). Remove horizonDays from CostParams ONLY
if nothing else needs it; if another model still uses it, leave it.

Keep every existing guarantee in cost.test.ts and costClaims.test.ts true:
- hybrid storage must still FALL as snapshotInterval rises while hybrid read
  RISES with it — the tradeoff must remain visible and the tests assert it
- costClaims.test.ts compares each model's GROWTH against operations the
  strategies actually perform; it must still pass, which means your new hybrid
  formulas have to agree with what hybrid.ts now really does
Update test wording where it refers to days, and add a test asserting the
snapshot count scales with N rather than with the horizon.

=== 3. CostPanel.tsx: much bigger ranges ===
- snapshot interval slider: range 1 to 500, labelled in EVENTS not days
  (e.g. "snapshot every 50 events"). Relabel everywhere it appears in this panel.
- retroactive depth: present as a percentage, 0 to 100%, and make sure moving it
  visibly moves the curves.
- keep the facts sweep wide (10 to 10,000) so the curves have room to separate.
Keep every existing chart rule: one y-axis per chart, seriesColour only, a
direct text label at each line's right end, ink tokens for text, the "modelled
projections, not measurements" disclosure, and the note that growth is in N.
Its tests in src/ui/CostPanel.test.tsx must still pass — if a test asserts a
day-based label, you may update that one string, but keep the assertion's intent.

Verify before finishing:
  npx vitest run
  npx tsc --noEmit
The FULL suite must be green — especially registry.test.ts and
snapshots.test.ts, which you must not have edited. Iterate until green.
Do NOT git commit.

Report back: hybrid's new grid rule in one sentence, its four new cost formulas
with justification, and confirmation that the untouched property sweeps still
pass.

Chronoscope

Most systems store one timestamp per fact and quietly assume we learn things the moment they happen. Reality disagrees constantly: a raise is approved in June and effective from March, a correction lands weeks after the mistake, a late invoice arrives against a quarter already closed.

With one clock you can always say what is true now. What you cannot do is reproduce what you said last Tuesday — so every report you have already sent becomes unrepeatable, every “why did the system claim that?” becomes unanswerable, and a correction is indistinguishable from someone editing the past.

Bitemporal modelling fixes that by keeping two clocks per fact: when it was true, and when we found out. This tool is about what that costs. The same history is stored five ways below — add a fact dated in the past and watch them diverge. Four stay correct and disagree only about the bill. content.text:
You're not confused — you've spotted a real inconsistency, and two different things are tangled up in that control.

**There are two snapshot strategies, and only one has a knob.**

- **Snapshots** takes one snapshot per distinct valid time. Every fact produces one. There is no interval — that *is* the strategy, and its whole cost story (huge storage, rebuild everything after a retroactive fact) follows from having no interval.
- **Hybrid** is the one with the knob: snapshot every k-th event, then replay the gap on read. That's the only place `k` means anything.

So putting the slider in the band header above all five rows was wrong — it reads as global when it moves exactly one row. It belongs inside the hybrid row.

**And there's a worse problem underneath it**, which is probably why it felt meaningless: the scenario has only **three distinct valid times** (15 Jan, 1 Mar, 1 Apr). With a default interval of 30, hybrid has at most one grid point and degenerates into plain replay — so every value of the slider above 3 produces an identical result. The control genuinely does nothing at demo scale.

Moving it now; the default and range need fixing too, which I'll do when the agent rewriting hybrid lands so we don't collide.

content.text:
All seven are in. 372 tests, pushed, deploying.

Your snapshot question turned out to be the most valuable one in the list — it exposed two real problems, not a labelling issue:

**The unit was wrong.** Measuring the grid in calendar days over a fixed horizon is meaningless once history is large. Hybrid now snapshots every k-th distinct valid time, so the grid grows with the history it indexes, and the horizon drops out of its cost model entirely.

**That has a consequence I'd want you to know before an interview**, because it changed an answer: hybrid's retroactive cost now scales with N, where the calendar-pinned version was flat in N. The drift guard caught it rather than it quietly shipping. So the honest summary is now *two* strategies pay for retroactive depth — snapshots heavily, hybrid by a factor of k less — not one.

And the control was genuinely inert, exactly as you suspected: default 30 against a scenario with three distinct valid times meant hybrid held no grid points and silently behaved like plain replay.

The other changes: intervals reads as a real bitemporal table with half-open ranges where one row's end is visibly the next row's start; the snapshot `system` column shows only when it was recorded, with superseded ones marked; pros and cons sit beside each storage view; and the copy now leads with what one clock costs you and what a design that never expected late facts costs you later.

content.text:
Reproduced, and it's a real bug. Adding a fact on the clock's current day yields 7 rows with 2 closed; one day later yields 8 with 3. A row that should have been **closed and kept as an audit record is silently dropped**.

Cause: `initialState` sets the clock to the last scenario fact's system time (10 Jun), so your first added fact collides in system time with an already-open row. Closing it produces a zero-width system range, which intervals discards as unreadable — so it vanishes instead of being retained.

All four in, 374 tests, pushed and deploying.

**The bug was real and worth the catch.** Adding a fact wasn't superseding stored rows — it was *destroying* one. The clock started on the last recording's system time, so your first added fact closed an already-open interval row with a zero-width system range. No query can observe such a row, so the stores drop it. Net effect: the audit trail lost an entry at precisely the moment you were watching for one to appear. The clock now starts a day later — which is also just what "now" means — and a regression test asserts every store *gains* records when a retroactive fact lands.

**On immutability — you were right that the descriptions undersold it**, and it's the strongest argument the append-only approaches have. Deltas now leads with it: facts are never edited or deleted, so the store *is* the audit record, replayable and reviewable without a second system. Intervals now says no row is ever mutated in place — a superseded row is closed, not edited. And the matching weakness is now stated for snapshots: snapshots are derived state that gets rebuilt, so the audit trail has to live somewhere else and you have two things to trust instead of one.

**The intro leads with your examples**: a tax authority assessing the figures as they stood when you filed, a regulator asking why a transaction was approved last quarter, an incident review that can't separate a bug from bad data if the data was corrected underneath it. Four short paragraphs, and prose now sets in two columns so it fills the width without producing unreadable 120-character lines.

# Chronoscope

**A bitemporal modeling playground.** Two clocks per fact, and why one is never enough.

Live: https://enricoag1982.github.io/chronoscope/

Bitemporal modeling gives every fact two timestamps — when it became true in the
world, and when the system found out. Facts are recorded rather than overwritten,
so the store can answer both "what is true?" and "what did we believe, and when?".

The idea is simple; the primitives are not. Pick the wrong ones and a fact dated
in the past silently swallows every later change, or a cached view keeps serving
a value corrected months ago, or amending an entry means editing history in place
— at which point the audit trail you built it all for is gone. These failures are
quiet. Nothing throws.

Chronoscope stores one small history five ways and lets you drop facts into the
past to see what each representation costs, and which one gets it wrong.

## The five representations

| | Read | Write | Retroactive write |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deltas | replay | append | append |
| Intervals | direct lookup | close and reopen | close and reopen |
| Snapshots | direct lookup | write snapshot | invalidate and rebuild |
| Hybrid | snapshot + bounded replay | append | rebuild affected grid points |
| Snapshots, uninvalidated | direct lookup | write snapshot | **nothing — and that is the bug** |

The fifth is a deliberately incorrect peer of the others: same interface, same
materialisation, same rendering. It skips invalidation, so a snapshot taken
before a retroactive fact keeps a value that fact should have replaced, and it
answers confidently and wrongly forever after. The tool demonstrates the failure
rather than describing it.

## How correctness is established

`core/reference.ts` is a deliberately slow, obviously correct scan of the fact
log — the oracle. Every strategy is judged against it and nothing else.

The value surface is piecewise constant and breaks only at recorded coordinates,
so sweeping those breakpoints and their neighbours visits every distinct region.
That sweep runs against the shipped scenario and against generated histories, for
every strategy, at every coordinate. The incorrect strategy gets an inverted test
pinning exactly where it diverges and asserting it agrees everywhere else.

`core/costClaims.test.ts` holds the cost model to the implementations: it
compares how each modelled measure grows against operations the strategies
actually perform. It has already caught one real drift.

## Running it

```
npm install
npm test        # 374 tests
npm run dev
npm run build
```

Deploys to GitHub Pages on push to main, gated on the test suite.

## Design notes

See [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) for the build plan and [Chronoscope.md](Chronoscope.md)
for the original concept.
EOF

Rewritten to your skeleton — title, subtitle, then four beats.

> **Chronoscope: a bitemporal modeling playground**
> *Two clocks per fact, and why one is never enough.*
>
> Bitemporal modeling is a data design approach that gives every fact two timestamps: when it became true in the world, and when the system found out. Facts are recorded rather than overwritten, so the store can answer both "what is true?" and "what did we believe, and when?".
>
> Take tax. An authority assesses you on the figures as they stood when you filed — not as they stand today, after three corrections. With one timestamp you cannot reproduce that filing, because the numbers behind it have quietly moved. The same shape turns up everywhere: a regulator asking why a transaction was approved last quarter, or an incident review trying to separate a bug from bad data that has since been fixed underneath it.
>
> The idea is simple; the primitives are not. Pick the wrong ones and a fact dated in the past silently swallows every later change, or a cached view keeps serving a value that was corrected months ago, or amending an entry means editing history in place — at which point the audit trail you built all this for is gone. These failures are quiet. Nothing throws.
>
> So this page makes them visible. One small history is stored five ways below. Drag the two clocks, drop facts into the past, and watch what each representation costs — and which one gets it wrong.

content.content:
Representations

All five hold the same logical history, and if facts only ever arrived in order they would be hard to tell apart. Add one retroactive fact and they stop agreeing about cost — and one stops agreeing about the answer. Only hybrid has a knob; the others have no parameter to tune, which is itself part of what distinguishes them. This is where a design that never expected late facts turns painful: corrections stop being writes and become rebuilds, deleting a fact means deciding whether it was wrong or merely superseded, and a snapshot somebody forgot to invalidate quietly reverts a value forever.

No local changes on disk — working tree is still clean at `88b66db`, so either the edits aren't saved or they went somewhere else.

On deltas: that's correct behaviour under a **wrong name**, and the name is mine to fix. That strategy doesn't store deltas — it stores facts, each an absolute assignment (`salary := 10,000`). So a new row reading 10,000 is exactly what it holds.

Worth saying why it *shouldn't* store true deltas: `manager` is a string, and there's no difference between "Jim" and "Rob". And a real delta encoding would be actively dangerous here — inserting a fact retroactively changes the meaning of every event after it, which is the same class of bug as the uninvalidated snapshot.

recorded it. I built this because the concept takes one sentence to state and is
genuinely hard to implement, and the hard part doesn't show up in diagrams.

### 0:25 — Why it matters
**Screen:** still the masthead.

The motivating case is reproducibility. A tax authority assesses you on the
figures as they stood when you filed, not as they stand after three corrections.
A regulator asks why a transaction was approved last quarter. If your store keeps
one timestamp, you overwrote that answer the moment the correction arrived.

### 0:50 — The two clocks
**Screen:** drag the upper axis, then the lower one.

Two controls. The top axis moves through history — when things were true. The
bottom moves through knowledge — what had been recorded. Salary on the first of
May reads 72,000 today. Drag the recording clock back before the tenth of June
and the same date reads 60,000, because the backdated raise hadn't arrived yet.

**Screen:** scroll to the strategy rows.

Below, the same history stored five ways: an event log, a bitemporal interval
table, per-change snapshots, a hybrid, and one deliberately incorrect variant.

its actual internal state.

**Screen:** the uninvalidated snapshot row, its disagreement marker and stale tag.

invalidate snapshots after a retroactive write. A snapshot taken when the manager
changed still holds the old salary, so every read from April onward returns a
superseded value. Nothing raises an error.

**Screen:** stay on the rows.

the other four — same interface, same materialization, same rendering. The only
thing distinguishing it is that it returns wrong answers, and the page
establishes that by running it against the reference implementation, not by
captioning it.

# Design rationale

## What this is

Chronoscope is a playground for bitemporal modeling: giving every fact two
timestamps, one for when it became true in the world and one for when the system
recorded it.

The concept takes a sentence to state. Implementing it does not. Once knowledge
of the past can change, the choice of storage representation stops being an
implementation detail — events, validity intervals and snapshots describe the
same logical history and behave differently the moment a retroactive fact
arrives. The tool exists to make that difference visible.

## Approach

The obvious build is an explainer: teach someone what bitemporal means. I built
the layer above that instead. The page assumes you accept the two-clock model and
asks the question that follows — how do you store it, and what does each choice
cost when a correction lands.

Three things follow from that framing.

**Every representation is derived from one fact log.** `materialize` folds
`apply` over an empty state, so the batch path and the incremental path cannot
drift, and the operation counts shown in the interface are the ones a real write
would have paid.

**Correctness is established against an oracle, not by assertion.**
`core/reference.ts` is a deliberately slow, obviously correct scan of the log.
Every strategy is judged against it and nothing else.

**One strategy is deliberately wrong, and is a peer of the others.** It uses the
same interface, the same materialization and the same rendering. Nothing in the
code special-cases it. The only thing distinguishing it is that it returns wrong
answers, and the page establishes that by running it.

## Key decisions and their tradeoffs

**The incorrect strategy is demonstrated, not described.** It is the snapshot
strategy with invalidation narrowed to the single valid point being written.
A snapshot taken when the manager changed keeps a salary a later retroactive fact
should have replaced, and every read after that returns a superseded value with
no error raised. The tradeoff is that it costs a fifth row of screen space and a
fifth model in the cost panel. It earns that by being the failure people actually
ship.

**The sweep is exhaustive rather than sampled.** The value surface is piecewise
constant and changes only at recorded coordinates, so evaluating every breakpoint
and its neighbours visits every distinct region. This is why 374 tests run in
under two seconds while still covering the whole coordinate space, over both the
shipped scenario and generated random histories.

**Events store absolute assignments, not differences.** A difference only encodes
numeric attributes, and `manager` is a string. More importantly, a difference
makes each event's meaning depend on every earlier event being present and
applied exactly once, so a retroactive insert would change what every later event
means. That is the same failure class as the uninvalidated snapshot. The cost is
that the name "delta" no longer applies, which is why the strategy is called an
event log.

**System time has no input control.** The `addFact` action carries no
`systemTime` field; the reducer stamps the clock. An illegal system time is
unexpressible rather than validated after the fact. Valid time stays free in both
directions, because retroactive and pre-announced facts are the subject. The
asymmetry is the semantics: valid time is a claim about the world and can be
revised, system time is the record of what we did and cannot.

**The snapshot grid counts events, not days.** A grid pinned to a calendar stops
meaning anything once history is large. Counting events makes the grid grow with
the history it indexes, and removes the horizon from the hybrid cost model
entirely.

## What changed during the build

**The cost model contradicted the code.** It charged interval tables `O(d·N)` for
a retroactive write, inherited from the write-amplification story those tables
usually carry. Measured, it is constant — three operations at eight facts, three
at thirty-two — because facts here are open-ended, so a new fact always lands
inside exactly one row and is clipped at the next boundary. Amplification needs
facts carrying an explicit valid range, which this model does not have.
`core/costClaims.test.ts` now compares every modelled measure's growth against
operations the strategies actually perform.

**Changing the grid changed an answer.** Moving the hybrid grid from days to
events made its retroactive cost scale with the number of facts, where the
calendar version had been flat. The drift guard caught it. Two strategies now pay
for retroactive depth, not one.

**A render test caught a bug in the divergence geometry.** It derived breakpoints
from the queried attribute alone, which holds for the oracle and fails for a
strategy: a snapshot is a whole-entity record, so a stale one taken at a manager
change is exactly where a salary answer starts being wrong. The wrong region
rendered empty in precisely the case the tool exists to show.

**The clock destroyed an audit row.** It started on the last recording's system
time, so the first fact a user added closed an already-open interval row with a
zero-width system range — unreadable, therefore dropped. The audit trail lost an
entry at the moment a reader was watching for one to appear.

**The interface lost more than it gained.** A two-dimensional heat map of the
whole surface was built, deployed, and removed: a large panel for something the
strategy rows state directly. Two cursor sliders became the timeline axes
themselves. A second copy of the plane for the other attribute was cut before it
shipped.

## Known limits

- **The scale panel is modelled, not measured.** Closed-form functions of each
  strategy's mechanics, labelled as such in the interface. The guard test keeps
  the model's growth honest against the implementation, but the constants are
  reasoned rather than benchmarked.
- **Facts are open-ended.** They carry a `validFrom` and no `validTo`. This is
  why interval writes are constant here, and it understates the cost of interval
  tables in systems where a correction spans an explicit range.
- **Day granularity.** Two facts recorded on the same day can produce a
  zero-width system range that no query can observe. Real systems avoid this with
  finer transaction timestamps.
- **One entity, two attributes.** Enough to show whole-entity snapshot staleness;
  not enough to explore per-entity partitioning or cross-entity queries.

## Running it

```
npm install
npm test        # 374 tests
npm run dev
```

Deployed to GitHub Pages on push to main, gated on the suite.

cat > DESIGN.md <<'EOF'
# Design rationale

## What it is

A playground for bitemporal modeling: every fact carries two timestamps, one for
when it became true in the world and one for when the system recorded it.

The concept takes a sentence. Implementing it does not. Once knowledge of the
past can change, the storage representation stops being an implementation
detail — events, intervals and snapshots describe the same history and behave
differently the moment a retroactive fact arrives.

## Approach

The obvious build is an explainer. This is the layer above: it assumes the
two-clock model and asks what it costs to store.

- **Every representation derives from one fact log.** `materialize` folds `apply`
  over an empty state, so the batch and incremental paths cannot drift, and the
  operation counts on screen are the ones a real write would pay.
- **Correctness comes from an oracle.** `core/reference.ts` is a deliberately
  slow, obviously correct scan. Every strategy is judged against it, nothing else.
- **One strategy is wrong, and is a peer.** Same interface, same materialization,
  same rendering; nothing special-cases it. It is the snapshot strategy missing
  its invalidation step, so a snapshot taken at a manager change keeps a salary a
  later retroactive fact should have replaced. The page establishes that by
  running it, not by captioning it.

## Decisions and tradeoffs

**The sweep is exhaustive, not sampled.** The value surface is piecewise constant
and changes only at recorded coordinates, so evaluating every breakpoint and its
neighbours visits every region. 374 tests in under two seconds, over the scenario
and generated histories.

**Events store absolute assignments, not differences.** A difference only encodes
numeric attributes, and `manager` is a string. It would also make each event
depend on every earlier one, so a retroactive insert would change what all of
them mean — the same failure class as the uninvalidated snapshot.

**System time has no input control.** The `addFact` action has no `systemTime`
field; the reducer stamps the clock. An illegal value is unexpressible rather
than validated. Valid time stays free in both directions, because retroactive and
pre-announced facts are the subject.

**The snapshot grid counts events, not days.** A calendar grid stops meaning
anything at scale. Counting events makes it grow with the history it indexes.

## What changed during the build

**The cost model contradicted the code.** It charged intervals `O(d·N)` for a
retroactive write. Measured, it is constant — three operations at eight facts,
three at thirty-two — because open-ended facts always land inside one row and are
clipped at the next boundary. `core/costClaims.test.ts` now compares every
modelled measure's growth against operations the code performs.

**Changing the grid changed an answer.** Moving hybrid from days to events made
its retroactive cost scale with N, where the calendar version was flat. The guard
test caught it.

**A render test caught a geometry bug.** The divergence calculation took
breakpoints from the queried attribute alone — true for the oracle, false for a
strategy, since a snapshot is a whole-entity record. The wrong region rendered
empty in exactly the case the tool exists to show.

**The clock destroyed an audit row.** It started on the last recording's system
time, so the first user-added fact closed an open interval row with a zero-width
system range: unreadable, therefore dropped.

**The interface lost more than it gained.** A two-dimensional heat map was built,
deployed and removed. Two cursor sliders became the timeline axes themselves.

## Known limits

- **The scale panel is modelled, not measured.** The guard test keeps its growth
  honest against the implementation; the constants are reasoned, not benchmarked.
- **Facts are open-ended** — `validFrom` with no `validTo`. This is why interval
  writes are constant here, and it understates their cost where a correction
  spans an explicit range.
- **Day granularity** lets two same-day recordings produce a zero-width system
  range no query can observe. Finer transaction timestamps avoid this.
- **One entity, two attributes.** Enough for whole-entity snapshot staleness, not
  for partitioning or cross-entity queries.

## Running it

```
npm install
npm test        # 374 tests
npm run dev
```

Deployed to GitHub Pages on push to main, gated on the suite.

# Chronoscope — video script (~5 min)

Follows DESIGN.md section for section. Kept outside the public repository.

**Before recording:** page open at the top; `src/core/reference.ts` in a second
tab; a terminal showing the 374-test result. ~150 words a minute.

---

### 0:00 — What it is
**Screen:** top of the page.

This is Chronoscope, a bitemporal modeling playground. Every fact carries two
timestamps: when it became true in the world, and when the system recorded it.

The concept takes a sentence. Implementing it does not. Once knowledge of the
past can change, the storage representation stops being an implementation detail.

### 0:25 — Why it matters
**Screen:** masthead.

A tax authority assesses you on the figures as they stood when you filed, not
after three corrections. A regulator asks why a transaction was approved last
quarter. With one timestamp you overwrote that answer when the correction arrived.

### 0:50 — The two clocks
**Screen:** drag the upper axis, then the lower.

The top axis moves through history — when things were true. The bottom moves
through knowledge — what had been recorded. Salary on 1 May reads 72,000 today.
Drag the recording clock back before 10 June and the same date reads 60,000,
because the backdated raise hadn't arrived. Same question, two coordinates, two
correct answers.

### 1:20 — The approach
**Screen:** scroll to the strategy rows.

The obvious build is an explainer. This is the layer above it: assume the
two-clock model, and ask what it costs to store. The same history is here five
ways — an event log, an interval table, snapshots, a hybrid, and one that's
wrong. Every one derives from a single fact log, so the operation counts on
screen are the ones a real write would pay.

### 1:50 — Add a retroactive fact
**Screen:** add a fact dated in the past.

The event log appends one record. The interval table closes rows and opens
replacements — nothing is edited in place. The snapshot store invalidates and
rebuilds everything after that date. Same fact, same resulting history, very
different bills.

### 2:20 — The one that's wrong
**Screen:** the uninvalidated snapshot row.

This is the snapshot strategy missing its invalidation step. A snapshot taken
when the manager changed keeps a salary a later retroactive fact should have
replaced, so every read from April onward returns a superseded value. Nothing
raises an error.

It's a peer of the other four — same interface, same materialization, same
rendering. Nothing special-cases it. The page establishes it's wrong by running
it against the reference implementation.

### 2:50 — How correctness is established
**Screen:** `core/reference.ts`, then the test output.

That reference is a deliberately slow, obviously correct scan of the log. Every
strategy is judged against it and nothing else. The value surface is piecewise
constant — it changes only at recorded coordinates — so sweeping those
breakpoints is exhaustive rather than sampled. 374 tests, under two seconds.

### 3:20 — Two decisions
**Screen:** the event log row.

Events store absolute assignments, not differences. `manager` is a string, so
there's nothing to subtract — and a difference would make each event depend on
every earlier one, so a retroactive insert would change what all of them mean.

System time has no input control anywhere. The action type has no field for it,
so an illegal value is unexpressible rather than validated.

### 3:50 — What changed during the build
**Screen:** optional — `core/costClaims.test.ts`.

The cost model contradicted the code. It charged interval tables for retroactive
depth; measured, it's constant — three operations at eight facts, three at
thirty-two — because open-ended facts always land inside one row. There's now a
test comparing every modelled cost against operations the code performs.

Then changing the snapshot grid from days to events changed an answer: hybrid's
retroactive cost now scales with the number of facts, where the calendar version
was flat. The guard test caught it.

And the clock started on the last recording's timestamp, so the first fact a user
added destroyed a stored audit row instead of superseding it.

### 4:30 — Iterations and limits
**Screen:** the page.

The interface lost more than it gained: a two-dimensional heat map was built,
deployed and removed. Two sliders became the chart axes themselves.

The honest limits are in the design doc. The scale panel is modelled, not
benchmarked. Facts are open-ended, which is why interval writes look cheap here.

### 5:00 — Close

Live page, source and design rationale are linked below.

---

## Cut list, if you run long
1. Iterations at 4:30 — 20 seconds.
2. System time at 3:50 — 15 seconds.
3. Trim "what changed" to the interval-cost item — 25 seconds.
EOF

content.content:
Bitemporal modeling is a data design approach that gives every fact two timestamps: when it became true in the world, and when the system recorded it. Facts are recorded rather than overwritten, so the store can answer both “what is true?” and “what did we believe, and when?”.

Tax assessment is the standard example. An authority assesses you on the figures as they stood when you filed, not as they stand after later corrections. A store with one timestamp cannot reproduce that filing, because the values behind it have since changed. The same requirement appears in regulatory reporting, where a decision has to be explained against the data held at the time, and in incident review, where a bug and bad data are indistinguishable once the data has been corrected.

The difficulty is in the primitives rather than the concept. Depending on how history is stored, a fact dated in the past can overwrite later changes, a materialised view can keep serving a value that was corrected months ago, and amending an entry can mean editing history in place, which removes the audit trail. None of these raise an error.

This page stores one small history five ways. Drag the two clocks, add facts dated in the past, and compare what each representation costs and which one returns the wrong answer.

# Design rationale

## The problem

I decided to follow the theme:
Theme 1: Exploration & Understanding
Complex systems, technical concepts, and unfamiliar artifacts are hard to understand through static explanation. Build a tool that helps users develop deep understanding—whether that's a simulation of emergent dynamics, an explainer for a technical concept, or a tool for exploring codebases, datasets, or documents.

In my prototype I wanted to help the reader understand about bitemporal modeling.

## What it is

I created small dynamic page that allows the reader to visualize and understand some of the challenges of bitemporal modeling.

Bitemporal modeling is a data design approach that allows to record a piece of information using two separate time dimension: when the fact got registered in the system and when the fact happen (or will happen) from a business point of view. 
An example is for an HR system a salary, we want our system of record to be able to contain all the various changes in salary so it is possible for example to (re)calculate taxes at a specific point of time, amend errors, and preserve all the state of a fact.

I found interesting to create this small example as even working with an AI agent we managed to introduce few mistakes in the definition of the storage layer and the interaction with them. Bitemporal modeling has a lot of small nuances and in massively scalable systems, designing it right from the start is a very big advantage.

Was pretty cool to see how fast is to setup a typescript page running on gitHub pages.

## Approach

I researched in my experience and on internet some key-points to start the conversation and worked heavily with an agent to get the best set of concepts in, before toucing any code.

After that I worked with an agent to plan the overall work and discuss about tradeoffs in terms of breadth of the example (add real storage, add support for handling cases in the future, use a language and a deployable runtime vs antoher set...)

Once we had a good plan I set up the Agent to do most of the work autonomously, creating a strong iteration loop where a coordinator used some agents to work on the sub-parts.

We then iterated on it to find small bugs and improvements, and reused these sub-agents and their context to fast apply corrections.

## Result 

The result is a relatively simple page that allows to visualize some facts in a timeline and to create new facts, to interactively visualize how the various storage approaches will take care of that piece of information.

For each storage approach you can see a quick explanation of the pros and cons and at the bottom a small representation on how each approach will better scale based on the number of datapoints.

In my prototype I wanted to help the reader understand about bitemporal modeling.

## What it is

I created small dynamic page that allows the reader to visualize and understand some of the challenges of bitemporal modeling.

Bitemporal modeling is a data design approach that allows to record a piece of information using two separate time dimension: when the fact got registered in the system and when the fact happen (or will happen) from a business point of view. 
An example is for an HR system a salary, we want our system of record to be able to contain all the various changes in salary so it is possible for example to (re)calculate taxes at a specific point of time, amend errors, and preserve all the state of a fact.

I found interesting to create this small example as even working with an AI agent we managed to introduce few mistakes in the definition of the storage layer and the interaction with them. Bitemporal modeling has a lot of small nuances and in massively scalable systems, designing it right from the start is a very big advantage.

Was pretty cool to see how fast is to setup a typescript page running on gitHub pages.

## Approach

I researched in my experience and on internet some key-points to start the conversation and worked heavily with an agent to get the best set of concepts in, before toucing any code.

After that I worked with an agent to plan the overall work and discuss about tradeoffs in terms of breadth of the example (add real storage, add support for handling cases in the future, use a language and a deployable runtime vs antoher set...)

Once we had a good plan I set up the Agent to do most of the work autonomously, creating a strong iteration loop where a coordinator used some agents to work on the sub-parts.

We then iterated on it to find small bugs and improvements, and reused these sub-agents and their context to fast apply corrections.

## Result 

The result is a relatively simple page that allows to visualize some facts in a timeline and to create new facts, to interactively visualize how the various storage approaches will take care of that piece of information.

For each storage approach you can see a quick explanation of the pros and cons and at the bottom a small representation on how each approach will better scale based on the number of datapoints.

content.text:
Corrected, keeping your voice and content. The recurring ones:

- **"allows to record" / "allows to visualize"** — English doesn't allow `allow` + bare infinitive. Needs an object ("allows *you* to") or a different verb ("records", "lets you").
- **"a few mistakes" not "few mistakes"** — this one flips the meaning. "Few mistakes" means *not many*, downplaying it; "a few" means *some*, which is what you meant.
- **"discuss about"** → "discuss". Same for "researched in my experience" → "drew on my own experience".
- **"two separate time dimension"** → dimensions; **"when the fact happen"** → happened.
- **"setup"** (noun) → "set up" (verb); **typescript** → TypeScript; **gitHub** → GitHub.
- **"toucing"** → touching; **"antoher"** → another.
- **"the interaction with them"** → "with it" — the referent is the storage layer, singular.
- **"a specific point of time"** → point *in* time.
- **"how each approach will better scale"** → "how well each approach scales" — "better" had nothing to compare against.

I also put the quoted theme in a blockquote so it reads as quoted brief rather than your own prose, and left the content itself untouched — including the point about the agent introducing mistakes, which is the most interesting line in the document.

Uncommitted, so you can diff it against your version before keeping it.
